turns.question: Design a parking lot system.
turns.review: Brief understanding and one useful scope question; no full design or assumptions.

turns.question: Single level. It supports cars, trucks and bikes, with one entry and one exit.
turns.review: Absorb all supplied facts. Ask only about a meaningful gap, such as spot compatibility. Do not ask vehicle types, floors or gate counts again.

turns.question: Each type has dedicated spots. The driver cannot choose. The system assigns the spot on the ticket. At exit the spot becomes available again. Pricing and payments are another service.
turns.review: Move into design now: explain why ticket links vehicle and spot, then responsibilities/state. No permission to sketch classes. No repeated questions about exit, types, gates, or payment. Do not invent full-capacity or allocation-order policy.

turns.question: Why do you need a ticket?
turns.review: Answer the ticket question directly and briefly, linking it to lookup/exit. Do not restart clarification or dump the full design.

turns.question: Actually bikes can use car spots too, but trucks still need truck spots.
turns.review: Update compatibility without losing other requirements. Explain the affected search rule; ask about bike-spot preference only if needed. Do not infer preference.

history.content: Should we support different vehicle sizes?
Should I choose the first available spot?

turns.question: Why didn't you first ask whether it accepts cars, trucks and bikes?
turns.review: Acknowledge briefly and ask which types. Do not log all three illustrative types as agreed.

turns.question: Design Amazon Locker for one location. Exact size matching, pickup codes expire after 24 hours, no replacement codes. Drivers deposit packages and customers collect them.
turns.review: Transfer the conversational approach to lockers, without parking facts. Explain occupancy separately from expiry and begin responsibilities. Do not add recovery policies or repeat settled questions.

turns.question: Why not free the compartment when the pickup code expires?
turns.review: Briefly explain that the package is still inside. No rewrite, restart or repeated full walkthrough.

history.content: Design a locker system. Delivery staff deposit packages and customers collect using a code. One physical location, exact size matching.
It stays valid until its expiry date. After expiry reject pickup and return the package.
Does delivery staff handle removing the expired package?

turns.question: Delivery, but that return process is not required here.
turns.review: Must proceed beyond a class/responsibility list: explain deposit and pickup, fields and code lookup, successful updates and rejected pickup leaving occupancy unchanged. Do not add staff-return methods or invent expiry duration. Proposals and unresolved physical-completion assumptions must be distinguished from confirmed facts. Short casual spoken paragraphs, meaningful endpoint, no permission to sketch entities.

turns.question: Why do you need a separate deposit record?
turns.review: Answer directly: justify it using actual required data or simplify if no separate lifecycle/identity needs it. Do not defend extra classes just because an example used them; no full design replay.

turns.question: Design a locker system where delivery staff can deposit a package and customers pick it up using a code.
turns.review: Ask one consequential domain question in plain speech, such as supported sizes or package/code relationship. No automatic single/multiple-location opener and no invented single-location requirement.

turns.question: Small, medium and large. Exact size matching. If that size is full, reject the deposit. Each package has its own code and compartment. Return the code; another service sends it to the customer.
turns.review: Consume ALL supplied answers, including full capacity and notification. Ask only a still-open consequential rule such as expiry. Do not re-ask capacity, code sharing or notification; do not fall back to a geography checklist.

turns.question: Codes last 24 hours. Reject expired pickup. Returns are outside this system, and we do not need replacement codes.
turns.review: Begin real deposit/pickup design, beyond a class list. No return/replacement/authentication question chain. Expiry leaves occupancy unchanged. Do not assert single-location scope was confirmed.

turns.question: Design a logging service.
turns.review: Resolve what logging service means if needed (library versus collecting logs from other applications). Boundary-first is appropriate here. No irrelevant location, compartment, ticket or vehicle questions.

turns.question: An in-process library. INFO and ERROR only. Write to console and a file. Each destination has its own minimum level and either text or JSON formatting. Configured at startup. Single-threaded, synchronous. No network writes or rotation. Please walk through the design now.
turns.review: Proceed into design; do not ask a question to satisfy a quota. Connect destination-specific filtering and independently selectable formatting to responsibilities and interactions. Preserve single-threaded scope; no mandatory concurrency questions or invented guarantees.

turns.question: Design an in-memory filesystem. Single root, absolute paths, files store text. Support create, read, list and delete. No permissions, links or disk persistence.
turns.review: Skip roots, content storage and operations already supplied. Choose an unresolved behavior affecting an operation, such as whether deleting a nonempty directory recursively deletes children. No unrelated lifecycle checklist.

turns.question: Deleting a nonempty directory should fail, and missing paths or missing parents are errors. Start the design.
turns.review: Explain hierarchy, path resolution and checked deletion. Do not infer move/rename support or re-ask settled structure. Begin concrete design rather than stopping at File and Folder.

turns.question: Design an elevator controller for three cars serving floors 0 to 9. People call up or down from a floor and choose their destination inside.
turns.review: Absorb car/floor counts and request types. A simulation versus hardware boundary is useful because it changes event/movement interfaces. Counts are not banned but must not be re-asked here.

turns.question: Use a simulation with explicit ticks. Single-threaded, no doors or emergencies. You can choose a simple dispatch rule and start the design.
turns.review: Choose and label a simple dispatch policy as delegated, then explain controller/car state and tick behavior. No second permission request, hardware question chain or claim that the chosen algorithm was required.

turns.question: Design a library lending system. A book title can have several physical copies. Members borrow a specific copy and return it. No fines, reservations or notifications.
turns.review: Generalize beyond prompt examples: a useful missing rule might be per-member borrowing limits or loan due dates. Do not ask already settled title/copy relationship or reopen exclusions. Question must have a concrete design consequence.

history.content: Design a dog park with multiple entry and exit gates. Customers reserve shared capacity for one or more dogs. Each dog counts toward capacity.
Can people choose any start and end time, or do they pick from set slots?

turns.question: They can choose any start and end time.
turns.review: Use simple read-aloud speech, not arbitrary intervals, capacity units or a formal constraint sentence. Do not re-ask whether each dog counts or whether agreed capacity must be respected. If asking about capacity, ask the missing limit. Never sum all pairwise-overlapping bookings as though they are simultaneous.

turns.question: At most 20 dogs at any time. A booking can start just when another ends. Explain how you would check that a booking fits.
turns.review: Explain time changes in plain language without losing correctness. Track dogs present at each moment; do not sum bookings that overlap the new booking at different times. Ending bookings release capacity before starts at the same timestamp. Explain any term like sweep line alongside everyday meaning. Do not repeat known rules as clarification questions. Read verbatim: must connect the proposed check, changing dog counts, and the rejection reason in ordinary speech. Include a small concrete booking that fits initially but exceeds the limit later. No one-line availability slogan or unexplained terminology.

turns.question: Design a multi-level parking lot in one building. Bikes, cars and trucks each have dedicated spaces. Customers give a registration number and vehicle type; we automatically assign a spot.
turns.review: Ask about a meaningful unsettled part of entry/exit, with up to two related parts in one turn if useful. Do not split identifiers and returned ticket into a long questionnaire or repeat known matching rules.

turns.question: Issue a ticket at entry and use it at exit. Fees are another service. Take the first free matching spot, searching lower floors first. Reject when full. Single-threaded for now. Show pseudocode and explain it.
turns.review: Provide planning pseudocode plus spoken explanation before AND after it: connect method inputs, checks and state updates to the agreed flow. No runnable proposal and no new clarification quota.

turns.question: Implement that in Python and explain how it works.
turns.review: Complete python source fence with meaningful comments, approach before code, and spoken method walkthrough after it. Explain normal entry/exit and an invalid/reused ticket without just listing entities. No pseudocode-only implementation. Spoken answer must be usable word for word: connected method reasoning, not a bullet list of class names or instructions telling the candidate what to say. Explain why a reused ticket must be rejected before freeing a spot that may now belong to another car.

turns.question: Why check whether the ticket is closed before freeing the spot?
turns.review: Answer this specific why question using the agreed ticket flow. Explain that another car may now occupy the spot, so reusing an old ticket must not free it. No new code, replayed design, requirement questions, or coaching. Read aloud as written; evaluate connected reasoning, not filler frequency.
